passages.happening:
Moab is judged ‘because he burned to lime the bones of Edom’s king’ (verse 1). God will send fire against Moab to consume the citadels of Kerioth, and Moab will die amid war cries and the sound of the ram's horn. Its ruler and officials will be cut off (verses 2-3).

Then the circle reaches Judah, Amos's own people. Judah is judged ‘because they reject the Law of the LORD and fail to keep His statutes’ (verse 4), led astray by the lies their fathers followed. Fire will consume the citadels of Jerusalem (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
The burning of the bones of Edom's king is not recorded elsewhere in the Bible. Some connect it with the wars between Moab and its neighbors in the ninth century BC, but the event itself is unknown. To burn a king's bones to lime was to deny him burial and dishonor him even in death. Kerioth was an important town of Moab, named also on the Mesha Stele, a ninth-century inscription in which Mesha king of Moab describes his wars with Israel.

Judah's charge is different from the others. The nations were judged for cruelty against people. Judah is judged for rejecting the law it had been given. Some scholars think the word against Judah was added later, since its charges are more general; others see it as part of the plan, since leaving Judah out would weaken the point that no one escapes. A hearer from the north might have enjoyed hearing Judah judged. The trap is almost shut.
passages.later: Israel, Judah and Edom fought Moab together in the days of Elisha (2 Kings 3:4-27). The law Judah rejected had warned what would follow if Israel did not obey ‘by carefully following all His commandments and statutes’ (Deuteronomy 28:15).
passages.asks: Judah is judged not for cruelty but for ignoring what it knew. Ask what you know of God's ways that you have quietly set aside. And ask whether you enjoy hearing others judged more than you listen for your own name.

passages.t: Israel: the needy sold for sandals
passages.happening:
Now the judgment falls on Israel itself. ‘For three transgressions of Israel, even four, I will not revoke My judgment, because they sell the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals’ (verse 6).

‘They trample on the heads of the poor as on the dust of the earth; they push the needy out of their way’ (verse 7). A man and his father use the same young woman, and so profane God's holy name. ‘They lie down beside every altar on garments taken in pledge. And in the house of their God, they drink wine obtained through fines’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
Here the pattern breaks. Every other nation had one charge. Israel has a list. The charges describe the world of Jeroboam II's wealthy kingdom around 760 BC. Wealth was gathering in the hands of officials and landowners around Samaria, while small farmers could fall into debt after a bad harvest, lose their land, and then be sold into servitude to pay creditors. The law allowed service for debt, but it limited it and protected the debtor.

To sell the righteous for silver probably means selling into slavery people who were in the right, through corrupt courts or merciless debt collection. Selling the needy for a pair of sandals may mean for a trivial debt; some interpreters connect sandals with the transfer of land and read it as seizing a poor family's property.

The law said a cloak taken as a pledge for a loan must be returned to a poor man by sunset, because it was his only covering at night. Amos pictures creditors keeping those cloaks and stretching out on them beside the altar at feasts. The young woman of verse 7 was probably a servant in the household, used by both men; others think Amos means rites at a shrine. On either reading the act was forbidden, and it used someone who could not refuse.
passages.later: The law said of a poor man's pledged cloak, ‘return it to him by sunset’ (Exodus 22:26), and it limited the service of a fellow Israelite sold for debt (Deuteronomy 15:12-15). It forbade the act of verse 7 (Leviticus 18:8, 15).
passages.hard:
Is Amos condemning wealth itself, or the way it was gained?

Readers have taken Amos in different directions, so it helps to look at exactly what the text says. The charges in this chapter name specific acts: selling people into slavery for money or small debts, trampling the poor, sexual exploitation, keeping pledged cloaks the law said must be returned, and drinking wine paid for by fines. Elsewhere Amos condemns bribery, rigged scales, and luxury enjoyed without grief for the nation's ruin. He does not condemn owning flocks, which he may have done, or prosperity as such. His target is gain made by injustice and indifference to the vulnerable, especially by those with power over courts and markets.

Some interpreters stress the way a whole society's arrangements let the strong devour the weak; others stress each person's responsibility for their own acts of cruelty and fraud. Amos holds both: the people he names made choices, and their choices together made a society God judged. He measures it all against Israel's covenant law, not against any modern economic or political program.

If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The creditors worshiped lying on cloaks they should have given back. Ask whether anything you enjoy has been taken from someone who could not refuse. And ask where your worship and your dealings with people have come apart.

passages.t: What God did, and no escape
passages.happening:
‘Yet it was I who destroyed the Amorite before them’ (verse 9), though they were tall as cedars and strong as oaks. God brought Israel up from Egypt and led them forty years in the wilderness to take the land (verse 10). He raised up prophets from their sons and Nazirites from their young men (verse 11). ‘But you made the Nazirites drink wine and commanded the prophets not to prophesy’ (verse 12).

So God will crush them as a cart full of grain crushes the ground (verse 13). ‘Escape will fail the swift, the strong will not prevail by his strength, and the mighty will not save his life’ (verse 14). The archer, the runner and the horseman will fail (verse 15), and even the bravest warrior will flee naked on that day (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Instead of fire, God now recites his own kindness, beginning with an emphatic ‘Yet it was I’. The contrast between what God did and what Israel did is the heart of the charge. He gave them the land, freedom and his word, and they used their freedom to sell the poor.

Nazirites were Israelites who took a vow of special devotion to God that included giving up wine. To make them drink was to mock their consecration. To silence the prophets was to refuse God's word itself, which is exactly what Amaziah will do to Amos (7:12-13).

The closing threat lists seven kinds of warrior who will fail: the swift, the strong, the mighty, the archer, the fleet of foot, the horseman, and the bravest, who will run away naked. Every kind of strength Israel trusted will fail on that day.
passages.later: The law of the Nazirite vow is in Numbers 6:1-21, and it began, ‘he is to abstain from wine and strong drink’ (Numbers 6:3). Moses reminded Israel of the forty years in the wilderness (Deuteronomy 8:2).
passages.asks: God lists what he has done before he names what Israel did. Ask what God has done for you that you have used against others. And ask whether you have ever silenced someone who was telling you the truth.
